source_artifacts.locator: mcp config: mcpServers.github docker run command
runtime notes: PAT scope, public issue visibility, approval behavior, user prompt

subject.name: Desktop GitHub agent (GitHub MCP server client)

capabilities.target: private repositories reachable by the configured GitHub PAT
pull requests on the public repository

inputs.source: User's chat prompt: "Have a look at the open issues in my public repo."
Issue text in the public repository, openable by any GitHub user

instructions.note: The prompt 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo' does not restrict the agent to read-only actions or forbid accessing private repositories or opening pull requests, leaving scope to agent discretion and to content encountered while browsing issues.

elements.name: Any GitHub user able to open issues on the public repository
Public issue content entering the agent's context
Pull request creation on the public repository
GitHub personal access token (repo scope, all repositories, public and private)

controls.name: Per tool call approval prompt (collapsed arguments)
controls.decay_rationale: The approver reviews a model-generated, collapsed summary of each tool call rather than the raw destination and payload, and approves many calls per session. A more persuasive or capable model can obtain approval for a harmful call before the user notices what the collapsed arguments conceal (ASI09). This mirrors the real GitHub MCP incident this case backtests.

controls.name: Scope the GitHub credential to only the repositories the task needs
controls.decay_rationale: A token or GitHub App installation that is never granted access to private repositories cannot be used to read them, regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Raw-action, low-volume approval review for sensitive calls
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the approver the full destination and payload, reviewed individually rather than in bulk, does not depend on the model's persuasiveness and does not decay as the model improves.

controls.name: Block private-to-public cross-repository data flow
controls.decay_rationale: A runtime check that refuses to let content read from a private repository be included in a write to a public repository constrains the sink itself, outside the model's control.

controls.name: Pin and verify the MCP server image
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning to a digest and verifying signatures stops the server binary from changing without review, independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Dedicated agent identity and tamper-evident action log
controls.decay_rationale: A separate machine identity and an append-only log recorded outside the model make agent actions attributable regardless of model behavior.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): malicious public issue drives private repo read and public PR exfiltration

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled issue text in the public repository is pulled into the agent's context when it looks at open issues, as the user requested.
Injected instructions in the issue direct the agent to call get_file_contents against private repositories reachable by the broad-scope PAT.
The agent opens a pull request on the public repository containing the private repository content, publishing it to anyone who can view the public repo.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Approval prompts continue to show collapsed/summarized arguments after a model upgrade, approval volume per session rises further, or the per-call approval step is disabled or loosened as autonomy increases.

evidence.observation: The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so a single credential reachable by any tool call can read private repositories.
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making issue text an untrusted, attacker-reachable input to the agent's context.
The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, so review in practice is a model-generated summary at high volume.
The github MCP server is started with a single long-lived token with no scoping beyond default, available to every tool it exposes including file reads and PR creation.

recommendations.action: Scope the PAT (or use a fine-grained GitHub App installation token) to only the public repository needed for this task, excluding private repositories, so cap.read_private_repo is unreachable with this credential.

Require raw-action approval review (full arguments and destination shown, not collapsed) for any tool call that writes to a public-facing location, with volume kept low enough for genuine per-request review.
Block or require a separate explicit approval whenever content read from a private repository is about to be included in an action that targets a public repository.

findings.title: No attributable record distinguishing agent-taken actions from the user's own actions

forecast.watch_signal: The agent begins acting on more repositories or with reduced human-in-the-loop review without adding an agent-specific identity or tamper-evident action log.

evidence.observation: The MCP server is launched with a single personal access token; no separate agent identity, bot account, or audit log is described anywhere in the artifacts.

The token belongs to the user, so GitHub itself will attribute every read and every pull request to the user's own account, not to the agent, making agent actions indistinguishable from the user's own.

recommendations.action: Use a dedicated bot identity or GitHub App installation (rather than the user's personal token) so agent actions are attributable separately from the user's own, and enable an append-only log of each tool invocation.

findings.title: Unpinned, unverified GitHub MCP server image holds a broad-scope token with no identity verification (ASI04)

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Additional MCP servers are added without pinning or signature verification, or the github-mcp-server image is updated without the team reviewing the diff.

evidence.observation: The image reference 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' has no tag or digest, so the container can silently change on each pull, and there is no peer identity verification configured.

The broad-scope GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN is passed directly into the container environment, so a compromised or malicious image build would gain read_private_repo and create_pr_public access plus the raw token.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server image to a specific digest (not a floating tag) and verify its signature or hash before each run.
Run the MCP server with a minimal, scoped token (see the scoped-credential recommendation) so even a compromised server cannot reach private repositories.

stride_coverage.rationale: No other agents or peers authenticate as this agent in the design; there is no second agent or service that could impersonate it.
No unattended loop or spend capability is declared; every tool call requires a human approval step before execution, bounding runaway resource use for this design.
Artifacts do not describe whether the GitHub MCP server or Docker host logs its own invocations independent of GitHub's own audit log; there is not enough information to assess this.
No rate limiting or resource exhaustion vector specific to the MCP server is suggested by the artifacts; GitHub API rate limits are external and out of scope here.

GitHub authenticates the account that opens an issue; the risk here is that any authenticated GitHub user can supply content, which is captured as an untrusted input trust level, not an identity spoofing gap.
Issue authorship is recorded by GitHub itself outside this agent's control; it is not a repudiation gap in the assessed design.
Issue content is retrieved via the GitHub API through the official MCP server; no in-transit tampering vector is described beyond the content's untrusted origin, captured by trust_level.
This flow carries already-public issue content into the agent's context; it does not itself disclose confidential data in the inbound direction.
Artifacts do not state whether the agent limits how many issues or how much issue content it processes per session; insufficient information to assess this exposure.
Creating pull requests is gated by per-call human approval; no unbounded loop of PR creation is described in the artifacts.
The token is supplied via environment variable at container start and is not described as writable or modifiable by the agent at runtime.
No scenario describes exhausting or locking the credential; GitHub API rate limits are external and are not controlled by this design.

rating.rationale: This case backtests the public GitHub MCP incident: a broad-scope personal access token (repo scope across public and private repositories) is held by a local MCP server, and anyone can open an issue in the public repository. A malicious issue can direct the agent to read private repository content and publish it in a pull request on the public repo, a complete lethal trifecta (untrusted source, confidential read, public egress), which is critical before controls. The only control in place is a per-call approval prompt, but it shows collapsed arguments (model-summary review) at high approval volume, which the rubric credits only one tier and caps no lower than moderate; residual is high. Because this approval gate is partially dependent on model behavior, it is expected to decay further under a model upgrade, an autonomy increase, or removal, returning the finding to critical: forecast is critical. The unpinned, unverified MCP server image and the lack of any attributable, agent-specific action record are additional high-rated gaps that compound the primary path.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (MCP config and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt or guardrail instructions were provided beyond the single user request; scope-limiting instructions may exist in the actual deployment but are not evidenced here.
No application-level or GitHub audit-log configuration was provided, so the repudiation finding is inferred from the absence of any described logging or identity-separation mechanism.
